sections.title: What haben means
sections.markdown:
**Haben** usually means **to have**. Use it to say what someone has: *Ich habe einen Schlüssel* (“I have a key”). It also appears in everyday expressions such as *Zeit haben* (“to have time”), *Hunger haben* (“to be hungry,” literally “to have hunger”), and *einen Termin haben* (“to have an appointment”).

In a present-tense statement, the form of *haben* changes to match the subject: *ich habe*, but *du hast*. This lesson uses *haben* as the main verb, not as a helping verb for the past tense.

sections.title: The complete present-tense pattern
sections.markdown:
| Subject | Meaning | Present form |
|---|---|---|
| ich | I | **habe** |
| du | you (one person, informal) | **hast** |
| er / sie / es | he / she / it | **hat** |
| wir | we | **haben** |
| ihr | you (several people, informal) | **habt** |
| sie | they | **haben** |
| Sie | you (formal, one or more people) | **haben** |

Memorize the contrasts **du hast**, **er/sie/es hat**, and **ihr habt**. The other forms are **ich habe** and **wir/sie/Sie haben**.

sections.title: Choose the form from the subject
sections.markdown:
First identify who has something. **Du** takes *hast* when speaking informally to one person; **ihr** takes *habt* when speaking informally to several. **Sie** with a capital S is formal “you” and takes *haben*. Lowercase **sie** can mean “she” (*hat*) or “they” (*haben*); the person or people meant determine the form.

A name for one person takes the same form as *er* or *sie*: *Mia hat Zeit.* Two named people take the plural form: *Mia und Ben haben Zeit.*

sections.title: Use haben in everyday sentences
sections.markdown:
In a simple statement, the subject commonly comes first and the conjugated verb second: *Wir haben heute Zeit.* An object or expression follows: *Ihr habt einen Schlüssel.* The words after *haben* depend on what you want to say, but they do not change the verb form—the **subject** does.

Do not use the English pattern “I am hungry” word for word with *haben*: German says *Ich habe Hunger.* Likewise, *Ich habe heute einen Termin* means “I have an appointment today.”

sections.title: Check the endings
sections.markdown: Avoid using the dictionary form *haben* for every subject: say *ich habe*, *du hast*, and *er hat*, not *ich haben*, *du haben*, or *er haben*. Also distinguish *du hast* from *ihr habt*: both mean “you have” in English, but German marks whether you are addressing one person or several. For formal “you,” use capitalized *Sie haben*.

worked_examples.title: I have a key
worked_examples.markdown: **Ich habe einen Schlüssel.** — “I have a key.” *Ich* takes *habe*.

worked_examples.title: One friend has time
worked_examples.markdown: **Du hast heute Zeit.** — “You have time today.” Addressing one person informally calls for *du hast*.

worked_examples.title: A neighbor has an appointment
worked_examples.markdown: **Mein Nachbar hat morgen einen Termin.** — “My neighbor has an appointment tomorrow.” One person takes *hat*, like *er* or *sie*.

worked_examples.title: We and you all
worked_examples.markdown: **Wir haben Brot. Ihr habt Käse.** — “We have bread. You all have cheese.” *Wir* takes *haben*; informal plural *ihr* takes *habt*.

worked_examples.title: They and formal you
worked_examples.markdown: **Die Gäste haben Hunger. Haben Sie auch Hunger?** — “The guests are hungry. Are you hungry too?” A plural subject takes *haben*. Formal *Sie* also takes *haben*, including in a question.

lesson.recap: Match *haben* to the subject: **ich habe; du hast; er/sie/es hat; wir haben; ihr habt; sie/Sie haben**. Use these forms for everyday expressions such as *Zeit haben*, *Hunger haben*, and *einen Termin haben*.
